--- title: "Monte-Carlo Sampling Distributions of the Residual-Field Mean" jupyter: python3 --- ```{=html} ``` This report is **descriptive only**. It measures the sampling distribution of the residual-field domain mean under two designs — sampling that is uniform with respect to the analysis measure, and sampling by advected virtual floats — and displays those distributions. It constructs no test statistic, reports no $p$-value, and draws no conclusion about the assumptions D1a/D1b or the permutation test of `theory.tex`. Standard errors are given so the reader can judge what the Monte Carlo does and does not resolve. # Estimand, truth, and estimator Let $\mathbb{P}$ be the normalized area $\times$ time probability measure on the Box B analysis domain: the base measure is surface measure restricted to the wet native GLORYS cells ($\mathrm{deptho} > 2000$ m, intersected with the data support), $A_j = e1t_j\,e2t_j$, tensored with counting measure on the $365$ days of the year and normalized. The target is the residual field's domain mean, $$\bar Z_k \;=\; \int_{\mathcal{X}} \tilde Z_k \, d\mathbb{P},$$ for each analysis year $k \in \{2015,\dots,2019\}$, where $\tilde Z_k$ is the year-$k$ OHC 0–2000 m field with the fitted mean field removed. A design is a finite point set $\{x_i\}_{i=1}^{n} \subset \mathcal{X}$; its estimator and bias are $$\hat Z^{(l,d)}_k \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tilde Z_k\!\left(x_i^{(l,d)}\right), \qquad B^{(l,d)}_k \;=\; \hat Z^{(l,d)}_k - \bar Z_k .$$ $\tilde Z_k$ is a simple function on the native $1/12^\circ \times$ daily grid, so evaluation at $x_i$ is the cell-day lookup of the cell *containing* $x_i$ — not an interpolation. No partition coarser than the data grid is introduced anywhere, so there is no quadrature remainder to carry. ::: {#tbl-truth .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
year Zbar (GJ/m2) sd_P(Z) (GJ/m2) Zbar / sd
2015 -0.240 6.565 -0.037
2016 -0.023 7.183 -0.003
2017 0.123 7.026 0.018
2018 1.173 7.146 0.164
2019 0.087 7.599 0.011
``` ::: ::: : Domain mean and dispersion of the residual field, by analysis year. {#tbl-truth} The mean field is fitted to a trend-plus-harmonics basis over 1995–2019, so $\bar Z_k$ would be exactly zero if the fit were exact on the analysis years. It is not: 2018 carries a residual $\bar Z_{2018} = +1.17$ GJ/m$^2$, or $0.16\,\sigma$. This is leftover mean-field misfit, not a property of the sampling, and it **cancels from $B$ by construction** — $B$ differences a sample mean against the domain mean of the same field, so any spatially uniform offset $\delta_k$ in $\tilde Z_k$ drops out identically. It is carried in @tbl-truth rather than assumed away. # The two ensembles Both use the same $1{,}895$ designs' worth of sample sizes, so they differ only in *where* the points sit. **Advective.** Virtual floats deployed uniformly with respect to $\mathbb{P}$ over a $\pm 8^\circ$ seeding margin and staggered across the year, advected through velocity year $l$, and retained only where they profile inside Box B. Ten velocity years $l \in \{2010,\dots,2019\}$ with $189$–$190$ independent deployment replicates each. Because the residual field exists only for 2015–2019, each velocity year is paired with all five analysis years: the pairing $l = k$ is **aligned** (flow and field are the same calendar year), all others **unaligned**, and 2010–2014 are unaligned for every $k$. **Uniform (U-full).** For each advective design, $n$ iid draws with cell $\propto A_j$ and $\mathrm{doy} \sim \mathrm{Unif}\{0,\dots,364\}$ — a genuine iid sample from $\mathbb{P}$, matched to that design's own $n$. By construction $\mathbb{E}[B] = 0$, so this ensemble is simultaneously the reference distribution and an end-to-end check of the gather, the day-of-year indexing, and the $\bar Z_k$ subtraction. ::: {#tbl-nsize .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}

Two consequences to keep in view: $\hat Z$ is a ratio estimator (the denominator is random), and the two ensembles are matched *conditional on* $n$. # Uniform sampling: the reference distribution ::: {#cell-fig-ref .cell execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Uniform-sampling estimates of the residual-field mean, one panel per analysis year. Red line is the truth Zbar_k. 1,895 designs, each an iid sample from P matched to an advective design's sample size.](mean_estimation_mc_files/figure-html/fig-ref-output-1.png){#fig-ref width=1429 height=319} ::: ::: ::: {#tbl-ref .cell execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}

The residual gap is a Jensen term: $\overline{1/n}$ is not $1/\bar n$, and the ensemble mixes designs whose $n$ spans two orders of magnitude. # Advective sampling ::: {#cell-fig-nsize .cell execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Profiles and distinct floats retained inside Box B, by velocity year. "Implied between-flow sd" is $\sqrt{\max(0,\,s^2 - \overline{\mathrm{se}}^2)}$, the part of the observed spread across the nine flows not accounted for by their own Monte Carlo error. {#tbl-aligned} Three features of @fig-heat and @tbl-aligned, stated as measurements: 1. The matrix is dominated by **column** structure. Every velocity year places roughly $+0.25$ GJ/m$^2$ on $\tilde Z_{2016}$ and roughly $-0.25$ on $\tilde Z_{2019}$, including 2010–2014, whose flows are five to nine years removed from those fields. 2. The **aligned** entries are $-0.031$, $+0.263$, $-0.015$, $-0.216$, $-0.368$ GJ/m$^2$ with Monte Carlo standard errors of $0.044$–$0.062$. Subtracting each column's mean over all ten velocity years leaves $[+0.001, +0.002, -0.069, -0.137, -0.109]$. 3. **Two different noise scales are in play, and they are similar in size.** Replication over $\sim 190$ deployments per cell shrinks the deployment component of the error to $0.04$–$0.06$ GJ/m$^2$. The observed spread across the nine unaligned velocity years is $0.031$–$0.059$ GJ/m$^2$ — the same order — so after removing each entry's own Monte Carlo error the residual between-flow standard deviation is $0$–$0.03$ GJ/m$^2$. Unaligned cells within a column are nearly interchangeable at this resolution; the flow year barely moves them. ::: {#tbl-deff .cell execution_count=10} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}
year median design effect sd Zhat advective sd Zhat uniform ratio
2015 1.952 0.561 0.417 1.346
2016 1.795 0.706 0.465 1.517
2017 1.990 0.664 0.445 1.493
2018 1.766 0.654 0.496 1.321
2019 1.827 0.702 0.522 1.345
``` ::: ::: : Within-design dependence. The design effect is $\sum_f \big(\sum_{i \in f} (\tilde Z_i - \hat Z)\big)^2 / \sum_i (\tilde Z_i - \hat Z)^2$, summing over floats $f$. {#tbl-deff} The advective histograms in @fig-grid are visibly wider than their uniform overlays. @tbl-deff attributes that: consecutive cycles of one float are near-replicates, so a design of $n$ profiles from $\sim 50$ floats carries roughly $n/1.9$ independent observations, and the advective ensemble runs $1.3$–$1.5$ times wider than its $n$-matched uniform counterpart. The width gap is dependence, not bias. # Temporal coverage versus spatial concentration An advected array does not sample the year uniformly. It ramps up from empty, and floats wander into the box over time, so the realized day-of-year marginal is heavily late-loaded (median day 250, 5th percentile day 90). Meanwhile the fitted mean field leaves a real seasonal residual: the spatial mean $\bar Z_k(d) = \int \tilde Z_k(\cdot, d)\, d\mathbb{P}_{\text{space}}$ varies over the year with a standard deviation of $0.4$–$0.7$ GJ/m$^2$. That combination alone biases $\hat Z$ without any spatial concentration whatever. Writing $\hat f^{(l,d)}$ for a design's empirical day-of-year distribution, the bias splits exactly in expectation as $$\mathbb{E}\big[B^{(l,d)}_k\big] \;=\; \underbrace{\sum_{d} \big(\hat f^{(l,d)}_d - \tfrac{1}{365}\big)\, \bar Z_k(d)}_{\text{temporal coverage}} \;+\; \underbrace{\Big(\mathbb{E}\big[B^{(l,d)}_k\big] - \sum_{d} \big(\hat f^{(l,d)}_d - \tfrac{1}{365}\big)\bar Z_k(d)\Big)}_{\text{spatial, given time}} .$$ The first term is what a design would suffer if it kept its own sampling days but drew its positions iid from $\mathbb{P}$ in space; it has the closed form above and is computed exactly, not simulated. The second is the remainder, attributable to *where* in the box the floats are on the days they sample. The split requires no assumption. ::: {#cell-fig-decomp .cell execution_count=11} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Total bias split into temporal-coverage and spatial-given-time components, per analysis year (panels) and velocity year (bars). Black dots are the total. The aligned velocity year is shaded.](mean_estimation_mc_files/figure-html/fig-decomp-output-1.png){#fig-decomp width=1418 height=361} ::: ::: ::: {#tbl-decomp .cell execution_count=12} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ```{=html}
year total B temporal spatial | time MC se column sd of temporal
2015 -0.031 -0.020 -0.012 0.044 0.001
2016 0.263 0.249 0.014 0.059 0.003
2017 -0.015 0.043 -0.058 0.061 0.002
2018 -0.216 -0.060 -0.156 0.058 0.002
2019 -0.368 -0.243 -0.126 0.062 0.002
``` ::: ::: : Decomposition of the aligned cells, and the variability of the temporal term across the ten velocity years. {#tbl-decomp} Two measurements: - **The temporal term is nearly identical across velocity years.** Its standard deviation down a column is $0.001$–$0.003$ GJ/m$^2$, against column means of up to $0.25$. Day-of-year coverage is a property of the deployment schedule and the array's ramp-up, essentially not of which year's flow the floats are pushed by. - **It accounts for most of the aligned bias in three of five years** — $95\%$ of 2016, $66\%$ of 2019, $63\%$ of 2015 — while in 2017 it carries the opposite sign to the total. What remains after removing it is $[-0.012, +0.014, -0.058, -0.156, -0.126]$ GJ/m$^2$. The temporal term is therefore close to, but not the same as, the column main effect of @fig-heat. Column means are $[-0.032, +0.261, +0.054, -0.079, -0.259]$ GJ/m$^2$ against temporal terms of $[-0.020, +0.249, +0.043, -0.060, -0.243]$: the two agree to within $0.02$ GJ/m$^2$, and the gap is a flow-independent *spatial* concentration effect of that size sitting underneath. The two routes to a residual — subtract the column mean, or subtract the closed-form temporal component — differ by that gap, and both leave 2017–2019 with the largest remainders. # Caveats - **One box.** Box B (35–45 N, 40–60 W) straddles the North Atlantic Current and Gulf Stream extension. Nothing here speaks to the quiescent Sargasso control (Box A), for which no residual field has been built. - **One flow realization per year.** The $\sim\!190$ replicates per cell are independent *deployments*; the velocity field is a single realization of that calendar year. Every standard error quoted is over deployment randomness only. - **$n$ is endogenous.** Retention inside the box is an outcome of the flow, so $\hat Z$ is a ratio estimator, the sample sizes differ systematically by velocity year (@fig-nsize), and the two ensembles are matched conditional on $n$. Design-weighted and profile-weighted averages of the temporal component differ substantially because $n$ and day-of-year coverage are strongly correlated ($r = -0.76$ for 2016); the design-weighted average is the one consistent with $\mathbb{E}[B]$ and is used throughout. - **The ramp-up is an artefact of the experiment.** Floats are released through the year into an initially empty box, which is what makes the day-of-year marginal so skewed. A spun-up array in steady state would have a flatter marginal and a correspondingly smaller temporal term. - **$\tilde Z$ inherits the mean-field fit.** The seasonal residual driving the temporal term is itself what the trend-plus-harmonics basis failed to absorb; a different mean-field specification would move it. @tbl-truth reports the fit's leftover offset per year.
